sections.summary: Introduces the extended mind thesis and argues through problem-solving cases that external operations can be cognitive when they play the same functional role as internal processes. The Tetris example shows physical rotation as an epistemic action that alters the world to aid recognition and search, warranting epistemic credit.
sections.title: Extended Cognition and Epistemic Action

sections.summary: Defines active externalism as a two-way coupling between organism and external entity, forming a coupled cognitive system. It contrasts this with Putnam/Burge passive externalism, where external features are distal and historical, and argues that coupled external features are active, causally relevant, and can be part of thought.
sections.title: Active Externalism and Coupled Systems

sections.summary: Addresses objections that extended processes are not truly cognitive because they are not conscious or portable. It replies that many cognitive processes are unconscious, and that reliable environmental coupling can make external resources part of the basic cognitive package. Evolution, development, and language can exploit such coupling, making extended cognition central rather than an add-on.
sections.title: Objections: Consciousness, Portability, and Reliable Coupling

sections.summary: Extends the argument from cognitive processes to belief. Inga retrieves a museum address from biological memory, while Otto relies on a notebook; the notebook plays the same role as memory, so Otto's belief is partly constituted by it. Twin Otto with an altered notebook differs in belief, showing that belief is not necessarily in the head.
sections.title: Otto's Notebook and Extended Belief

sections.summary: Defends extended belief against objections based on reliability, temporary disconnection, perceptual access, and phenomenology. It argues that Otto's access need only be reliable enough, occasional unavailability does not erase belief, and perceptual or phenomenological differences are shallow compared with the shared functional role of notebook and memory.
sections.title: Defending Extended Belief Against Objections

sections.summary: Explores how far extended belief and mind can go. It lists features that make Otto's case clear, allows indeterminate intermediate cases, and extends the account to socially distributed cognition and the self. Language, trust, reliance, and accessibility support social extension, while the extended self follows from treating Otto's notebook as central to his cognitive identity.
sections.title: Beyond the Outer Limits: Criteria, Social Extension, and the Extended Self
